name: Influenza

past_medical_history.chronic_conditions: COPD, asthma, heart disease, diabetes increase severity

medications: symptomatic treatment with acetaminophen or NSAIDs

physical_exam.general: appears ill, fatigued, uncomfortable

respiratory.inspection: normal respiratory effort
respiratory.auscultation: clear lungs or diffuse rhonchi, crackles if pneumonia

cardiovascular.auscultation: normal or tachycardic

rapid_influenza_test.result: positive for Influenza A or B
rapid_influenza_test.interpretation: 50-70% sensitivity, high specificity. False negatives common.

pcr_influenza.interpretation: Gold standard, high sensitivity and specificity

chest_xray.result: clear or bilateral infiltrates if influenza pneumonia
chest_xray.interpretation: Only if suspect pneumonia - dyspnea, hypoxemia

viral_panel.result: may show other respiratory viruses if influenza negative
viral_panel.interpretation: Broader testing if influenza test negative

teaching_points: Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) most effective if started within 48 hours of symptom onset
Treat high-risk patients empirically without waiting for test results
Annual vaccination is best prevention strategy
Complications: primary influenza pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia, myositis, myocarditis
Distinguish from COVID-19: both can present similarly, test if unclear
key_features: Abrupt onset of high fever and severe myalgias

name: Acute Pharyngitis (Strep Throat)

primary_symptoms.fever: yes if bacterial, less common if viral

physical_exam.general: appears uncomfortable, may have muffled voice

head_and_neck.oropharynx: pharyngeal erythema, tonsillar exudates (white/yellow), petechiae on soft palate

physical_exam.skin: scarlatiniform rash if scarlet fever - sandpaper texture, spares face

rapid_strep_antigen_test.interpretation: 85-95% sensitivity, high specificity. Treat if positive.

throat_culture.result: Group A Strep growth or no growth
throat_culture.interpretation: Gold standard, send if rapid test negative and high suspicion

centor_score.result: 0-4 points: fever, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough
centor_score.interpretation: Score 3-4: test and treat. Score 0-1: no testing needed.

monospot.interpretation: Consider if atypical presentation, fatigue, splenomegaly

cbc.result: leukocytosis if bacterial, atypical lymphocytes if mono

essential_questions: presence of cough or cold symptoms

teaching_points: Centor criteria guide testing: fever, exudates, nodes, no cough
Treat confirmed Strep with penicillin or amoxicillin to prevent rheumatic fever
Viral pharyngitis is more common - antibiotics not indicated
Avoid amoxicillin if mono suspected - causes rash
GAS pharyngitis complications: rheumatic fever, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, peritonsillar abscess
key_features: Acute onset sore throat with fever
Absence of cough or cold symptoms

name: Pulmonary Edema (Cardiogenic)

patient_demographics.appearance: appears severely distressed, sitting upright, gasping

past_medical_history.heart_failure: yes, known systolic or diastolic dysfunction

vital_signs.blood_pressure: elevated 180/100 or low if cardiogenic shock

physical_exam.general: severe respiratory distress, diaphoretic, sitting bolt upright, tripod position

respiratory.inspection: labored breathing, use of accessory muscles
respiratory.auscultation: bilateral crackles, diffuse rales from bases to apices, wheezing (cardiac asthma)

cardiovascular.auscultation: S3 gallop, tachycardic, possibly murmur if valvular

physical_exam.extremities: cool if low output, peripheral edema, pitting

chest_xray.result: bilateral infiltrates in butterfly pattern, Kerley B lines, cephalization, cardiomegaly, pleural effusions

bnp_or_ntprobnp.interpretation: Heart failure present, excludes non-cardiac causes

ecg.result: may show LVH, ischemia, arrhythmia, previous MI
ecg.interpretation: Identifies precipitating factors or underlying heart disease

troponin.result: may be elevated if ischemic etiology

echocardiogram.result: reduced EF if systolic dysfunction, diastolic dysfunction, valvular disease

abg.result: severe hypoxemia, respiratory alkalosis initially, then acidosis

teaching_points: BNP >500 or NT-proBNP >900 indicates heart failure
Treatment: oxygen, IV diuretics, nitrates, consider CPAP/BiPAP
Identify and treat precipitating cause (ischemia, arrhythmia, infection)
Distinguish from ARDS: BNP low in ARDS, normal heart size
LMNOP mnemonic: Lasix, Morphine, Nitrates, Oxygen, Position (upright)

name: Spontaneous Pneumothorax

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: sudden onset chest pain and shortness of breath

patient_demographics.age_range: 20-40 for primary spontaneous, any age for secondary
patient_demographics.appearance: appears anxious, tachypneic, tall thin habitus if primary

past_medical_history.underlying_lung_disease: COPD, cystic fibrosis, asthma for secondary

vital_signs.blood_pressure: normal or decreased if tension PTX

physical_exam.general: anxious, tachypneic, sitting upright, leaning toward affected side

respiratory.inspection: decreased chest wall movement on affected side, tracheal deviation away from affected side if tension
respiratory.palpation: decreased tactile fremitus on affected side
respiratory.auscultation: decreased or absent breath sounds on affected side

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, may be muffled if large

physical_exam.signs_of_tension: tracheal deviation, JVD, hypotension, absent breath sounds - medical emergency

chest_xray.result: visceral pleural line separated from chest wall, absent lung markings peripherally

expiratory_chest_xray.result: more apparent pleural line on expiration

ct_chest.result: clearly defines pneumothorax and any underlying blebs/bullae
ct_chest.interpretation: Gold standard, detects occult PTX, identifies blebs

ultrasound.result: absence of lung sliding, absent comet-tail artifacts

teaching_points: Tension pneumothorax is clinical diagnosis - needle decompression before imaging
Primary spontaneous PTX occurs in tall thin young males at rest
Pneumothorax >2cm or symptomatic requires intervention (aspiration or chest tube)
Recurrence rate 30-50% after first episode, higher with subsequent episodes
Avoid flying or scuba diving for 2 weeks after resolution
key_features: Decreased breath sounds on affected side
Visceral pleural line on chest X-ray

name: Acute Bronchitis

symptom_onset.progression: URI symptoms improving, but cough persisting

physical_exam.general: well-appearing, no distress except during coughing fits

respiratory.inspection: normal respiratory effort
respiratory.auscultation: clear lung fields or scattered rhonchi that clear with coughing, no wheezing, no crackles

cardiovascular.auscultation: regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs

physical_exam.ent: may have pharyngeal erythema, no exudates

chest_xray.result: clear lung fields, no infiltrates
chest_xray.interpretation: Rules out pneumonia - not routinely indicated

rapid_viral_panel.interpretation: Identifies viral etiology - not routinely needed

procalcitonin.interpretation: Suggests viral rather than bacterial - helps avoid unnecessary antibiotics

teaching_points: Acute bronchitis is typically viral - antibiotics NOT indicated
Cough may persist 3-4 weeks after infection resolves
Chest X-ray only needed if suspect pneumonia (fever, tachypnea, abnormal lung sounds)
Treatment is symptomatic: antitussives, NSAIDs, hydration
Most common cause of inappropriate antibiotic prescribing in primary care
key_features: No infiltrate on chest X-ray if done

name: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: shortness of breath and chronic cough

patient_demographics.appearance: appears chronically ill, barrel-chested, pursed-lip breathing

symptom_onset.timing: years, with acute worsening over 3 days

social_history.smoking: 40+ pack-year history, current or former smoker

physical_exam.general: thin, cachetic, barrel-chested, pursed-lip breathing, tripod position

respiratory.inspection: prolonged expiratory phase, use of accessory muscles, increased AP diameter
respiratory.auscultation: decreased breath sounds, distant, scattered wheezes, coarse crackles if infection

cardiovascular.inspection: JVP may be elevated if cor pulmonale
cardiovascular.auscultation: distant heart sounds, may have RV heave, loud P2 if pulmonary hypertension

physical_exam.extremities: peripheral cyanosis, clubbing in advanced disease, pedal edema if cor pulmonale

spirometry.result: FEV1/FVC <70%, FEV1 <80% predicted, minimal reversibility with bronchodilator
spirometry.interpretation: Fixed obstructive pattern, GOLD stage based on FEV1

chest_xray.result: hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm, increased retrosternal airspace, bullae

abg.result: chronic hypoxemia, hypercapnia in advanced disease, compensated respiratory acidosis
abg.interpretation: Type II respiratory failure if chronic CO2 retention

cbc.result: polycythemia if chronic hypoxemia, elevated WBC if infection

alpha1_antitrypsin_level.interpretation: Screen if young age (<45) or minimal smoking history

ecg.result: right axis deviation, RVH, P pulmonale if cor pulmonale
ecg.interpretation: Right heart strain from pulmonary hypertension

ct_chest.result: centrilobular emphysema, panlobular if alpha1 deficiency, bronchial wall thickening
ct_chest.interpretation: Defines extent and distribution of disease

teaching_points: FEV1/FVC <70% defines obstruction, FEV1 stages severity (GOLD classification)
Smoking cessation is most important intervention to slow progression
LABA/LAMA combination is first-line for symptomatic patients
Home oxygen if PaO2 <55 or O2 sat <88% at rest
Exacerbations defined by increased dyspnea, sputum volume, or sputum purulence

name: Asthma

patient_demographics.sex: equal, slight male predominance in children

primary_symptoms.cough: yes, dry or with clear sputum

physical_exam.general: anxious, sitting upright, using accessory muscles

respiratory.inspection: prolonged expiratory phase, tripod position
respiratory.auscultation: diffuse expiratory wheezing, decreased air entry if severe

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, regular, no murmurs

physical_exam.other_findings: may have nasal polyps, eczematous rash

peak_flow.result: 40% of predicted, improved to 75% after bronchodilator

spirometry.result: FEV1/FVC ratio <70%, FEV1 improves >12% after bronchodilator

chest_xray.result: hyperinflation, no infiltrates

abg.result: respiratory alkalosis initially, then respiratory acidosis if severe

teaching_points: Asthma is reversible airway obstruction vs COPD which is fixed
Peak flow <50% predicted indicates severe exacerbation
Silent chest is ominous sign requiring immediate intervention
Inhaled corticosteroids are cornerstone of chronic management
Assess asthma control using ACT (Asthma Control Test) score
key_features: Worse at night or with exercise
Triggered by allergens, cold air, or exercise

name: Community-Acquired Pneumonia

physical_exam.general: ill-appearing, tachypneic

respiratory.inspection: increased work of breathing
respiratory.palpation: increased tactile fremitus over affected area
respiratory.auscultation: crackles, bronchial breath sounds, egophony

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, regular, no murmurs

chest_xray.result: lobar consolidation in right lower lobe with air bronchograms

blood_culture.result: positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae in 20% of cases

teaching_points: CURB-65 score determines outpatient vs inpatient management
Streptococcus pneumoniae is most common cause of CAP
Empiric antibiotics should cover typical and atypical pathogens
Chest X-ray may lag clinical improvement by several days
Parapneumonic effusion requires thoracentesis if moderate or large
key_features: Acute onset of cough, fever, and dyspnea
Crackles and bronchial breath sounds on examination

name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

patient_demographics.appearance: critically ill, intubated or requiring intubation

physical_exam.general: critically ill, intubated, sedated

respiratory.inspection: mechanically ventilated, high PEEP requirements
respiratory.auscultation: diffuse crackles bilaterally, decreased breath sounds if severe

cardiovascular.inspection: JVP normal (distinguishes from cardiogenic pulmonary edema)
cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, no S3 gallop

physical_exam.other_findings: signs of underlying condition (sepsis, trauma, etc.)

chest_xray.result: bilateral diffuse infiltrates, 'white out' appearance, no cardiomegaly

abg.interpretation: Berlin criteria: defines ARDS severity based on P/F ratio

bnp.interpretation: Excludes heart failure as primary cause

bronchoscopy.result: may show diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, infection, or clear airways

cultures.result: may identify causative organism if infectious

essential_exams: cardiovascular examination to exclude heart failure

teaching_points: Berlin criteria: acute onset (<7 days), bilateral infiltrates, P/F <300, not fully explained by cardiac failure
Severity: mild (P/F 200-300), moderate (P/F 100-200), severe (P/F <100)
Treatment: lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volume 6ml/kg, plateau pressure <30)
Prone positioning improves oxygenation and mortality in severe ARDS
Mortality: 30-40% overall, higher in severe ARDS
key_features: Acute onset within 7 days of known insult
Not fully explained by heart failure

name: Pneumococcal Pneumonia

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: sudden onset fever, cough, and chest pain

patient_demographics.appearance: appears acutely ill, febrile, shaking chills

physical_exam.general: acutely ill, toxic appearance, rigors

respiratory.inspection: splinting on affected side, decreased chest expansion
respiratory.auscultation: bronchial breath sounds, crackles, egophony, whispered pectoriloquy

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, regular

chest_xray.result: lobar consolidation, typically single lobe, air bronchograms

teaching_points: Most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia requiring hospitalization
Classic presentation: single rigor, rusty sputum, lobar consolidation
Pneumococcal vaccine (PPSV23, PCV13) recommended for high-risk patients
Complications: empyema, bacteremia, meningitis, endocarditis
Treatment: ceftriaxone or levofloxacin; penicillin if susceptible
key_features: Abrupt onset with single shaking chill

name: Pleural Effusion

patient_demographics.appearance: appears mildly dyspneic, may lean toward affected side

physical_exam.general: comfortable at rest or mildly dyspneic

respiratory.inspection: decreased chest wall movement on affected side
respiratory.auscultation: decreased or absent breath sounds, egophony above effusion

cardiovascular.inspection: JVD if CHF, no JVD if other causes
cardiovascular.auscultation: may have S3 if CHF

chest_xray.result: blunting of costophrenic angle, meniscus sign, if large: opacification of hemithorax

ct_chest.result: fluid collection, identifies underlying lung pathology

pleural_fluid_analysis.result: protein, LDH, glucose, pH, cell count, cultures, cytology

teaching_points: Light's criteria distinguishes transudate from exudate
Transudate: CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome (treat underlying cause)
Exudate: infection, malignancy, PE (requires further workup)
Thoracentesis indicated if >1cm on lateral decubitus film or unknown etiology
Complicated parapneumonic effusion requires chest tube drainage
key_features: Dullness to percussion at lung base
Blunted costophrenic angle on chest X-ray

name: Lung Abscess

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: prolonged fever and cough with foul-smelling sputum

patient_demographics.appearance: appears chronically ill, cachectic, poor dentition

physical_exam.general: chronically ill appearing, cachectic, poor dentition, fetor oris

respiratory.inspection: may have splinting
respiratory.percussion: dullness if consolidation, tympany if air-filled cavity
respiratory.auscultation: crackles, bronchial breath sounds, amphoric breath sounds over cavity

cardiovascular.auscultation: normal or tachycardic

chest_xray.result: thick-walled cavity with air-fluid level, typically in dependent segments (posterior upper lobe, superior lower lobe)

ct_chest.result: well-defined cavity with air-fluid level, thick irregular wall, surrounding consolidation
ct_chest.interpretation: Better defines anatomy, rules out malignancy

sputum_culture.result: mixed anaerobes, Streptococcus milleri group, sometimes Staph aureus or Klebsiella

bronchoscopy.result: may obtain samples, rule out obstruction

teaching_points: Aspiration is most common cause - anaerobic bacteria from oral flora
Located in dependent lung segments: posterior upper lobe, superior lower lobe
Treatment: prolonged antibiotics (4-6 weeks), clindamycin or amoxicillin-clavulanate
Complications: empyema, bronchopleural fistula, hemoptysis
Bronchoscopy indicated if suspect obstruction or malignancy
key_features: History of aspiration or altered consciousness

name: Acute Sinusitis

symptom_onset.progression: worsening or not improving after initial URI

physical_exam.general: appears uncomfortable, no distress

head_and_face.inspection: may have periorbital edema if ethmoid sinusitis
head_and_face.palpation: tenderness over maxillary or frontal sinuses

physical_exam.teeth: may have tenderness to upper teeth percussion

clinical_diagnosis.result: ≥2 major criteria or 1 major + ≥2 minor criteria
clinical_diagnosis.interpretation: Major: purulent discharge, facial pain, nasal obstruction. Minor: fever, headache, dental pain

ct_sinuses.interpretation: Gold standard but not routinely needed; use if complications suspected or refractory

nasal_endoscopy.result: purulent discharge from middle meatus, mucosal edema

sinus_xray.interpretation: Limited utility, CT preferred if imaging needed

culture.interpretation: Not routinely needed; requires sinus puncture for accuracy

Bacterial sinusitis: symptoms >10 days or worsening after 5-7 days

essential_tests: CT only if complications or refractory

teaching_points: Most cases are viral - antibiotics only if bacterial criteria met
Bacterial criteria: symptoms >10 days OR worsening after initial improvement OR severe symptoms with high fever
First-line antibiotic: amoxicillin-clavulanate
Imaging not needed for uncomplicated acute sinusitis
Red flags: periorbital edema, vision changes, severe headache (orbital/intracranial complications)
key_features: Symptoms >7 days or worsening after initial improvement

name: Croup (Acute Obstructive Laryngitis)

physical_exam.general: alert, anxious, prefers sitting upright, no toxic appearance

respiratory.inspection: inspiratory stridor, suprasternal and intercostal retractions, accessory muscle use
respiratory.auscultation: transmitted upper airway sounds, clear lung fields, no wheezing

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, regular

clinical_diagnosis.result: barky cough, stridor, hoarseness in child 6mo-3yr

neck_xray_ap.interpretation: Classic finding but not required for diagnosis

neck_xray_lateral.interpretation: Rules out epiglottitis or retropharyngeal abscess

viral_pcr.result: parainfluenza virus most common, also RSV, influenza

teaching_points: Parainfluenza virus is most common cause (75% of cases)
Treatment: dexamethasone 0.6mg/kg (single dose), nebulized epinephrine if severe
Steeple sign on X-ray is classic but not required for diagnosis
Mild croup can be managed at home with cool mist therapy
Red flags requiring immediate intervention: cyanosis, altered mental status, inability to speak

name: Respiratory Failure

patient_demographics.appearance: critically ill, altered mental status, cyanotic

symptom_onset.timing: acute or chronic with acute decompensation

vital_signs.heart_rate: tachycardic >120 or bradycardic if near arrest

physical_exam.general: severe distress, altered mental status, obtunded, cyanotic, diaphoretic

respiratory.inspection: accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, chest-abdominal dyssynchrony
respiratory.auscultation: variable - absent breath sounds, crackles, wheezing, or decreased air entry

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic or irregular

arterial_blood_gas.result: Type I: PaO2 <60, normal/low CO2. Type II: PaO2 <60, PaCO2 >50
arterial_blood_gas.interpretation: Defines type and severity of respiratory failure

chest_xray.result: variable - infiltrates, effusions, pneumothorax, hyperinflation

ecg.result: may show arrhythmia, ischemia, RV strain

Type I (hypoxemic): causes: pneumonia, PE, ARDS, pulmonary edema
Type II (hypercapnic): causes: COPD, neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation, drug overdose

teaching_points: Type I (hypoxemic): failure of oxygenation, treat with supplemental O2, PEEP
Type II (hypercapnic): failure of ventilation, treat underlying cause, may need mechanical ventilation
Acute on chronic: baseline elevated CO2, look for metabolic compensation (elevated HCO3)
Indications for intubation: inability to protect airway, PaO2 <50 despite O2, PaCO2 >60 with pH <7.25
Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) can prevent intubation in COPD and CHF
key_features: Severe dyspnea with altered mental status
Type I: normal/low CO2; Type II: elevated CO2

name: Bronchiectasis

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: chronic productive cough with recurrent infections

patient_demographics.appearance: chronically ill, frequent coughing with sputum production

physical_exam.general: chronically ill appearing, frequent productive cough

respiratory.inspection: increased AP diameter sometimes
respiratory.auscultation: coarse crackles at bases, rhonchi, squeaks, wheezes

cardiovascular.auscultation: may have loud P2 if cor pulmonale

hrct_chest.result: bronchial dilation >1.5x adjacent artery, lack of bronchial tapering, signet ring sign

chest_xray.result: increased markings, tramlines, ring shadows, may be normal

sputum_culture.result: Pseudomonas, H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, NTM (non-tuberculous mycobacteria)

immunoglobulin_levels.result: low IgG, IgA, or IgM if immunodeficiency

teaching_points: HRCT with bronchial dilation >1.5x adjacent artery is diagnostic
Signet ring sign: dilated bronchus next to pulmonary artery
Treatment: airway clearance, antibiotics for exacerbations, treat underlying cause
Pseudomonas colonization indicates more severe disease
Massive hemoptysis may require bronchial artery embolization
key_features: Chronic productive cough with copious sputum

name: Empyema (Pyothorax)

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: persistent fever and chest pain despite pneumonia treatment

primary_symptoms.fever: yes, persistent or spiking despite antibiotics

physical_exam.general: appears ill, toxic, diaphoretic

respiratory.inspection: decreased chest expansion on affected side
respiratory.auscultation: decreased or absent breath sounds, pleural rub sometimes

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, regular

physical_exam.other: may have weight loss if chronic

chest_xray.result: pleural effusion, may see loculations or air-fluid level if bronchopleural fistula
chest_xray.interpretation: Shows effusion but cannot distinguish from simple effusion

ultrasound_chest.result: complex effusion with septations, echogenic debris

ct_chest_with_contrast.result: pleural thickening, split pleura sign (enhancing visceral and parietal pleura)

pleural_fluid_analysis.result: pH <7.2, glucose <60, LDH >1000, WBC >50,000 with PMN predominance, positive gram stain or culture

teaching_points: Empyema = pus in pleural space, requires drainage
Light's criteria for exudate, but empyema needs: pH <7.2, glucose <60, or positive gram stain
Treatment: antibiotics PLUS drainage (chest tube, VATS, or open decortication)
Organisms: Strep pneumoniae, Staph aureus, anaerobes if aspiration
Three stages: exudative (thin fluid), fibrinopurulent (loculations), organizing (pleural peel)
key_features: Split pleura sign on contrast CT

name: Interstitial Lung Disease (Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis)

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: progressive shortness of breath and dry cough

patient_demographics.appearance: appears chronically ill, tachypneic, uses accessory muscles

primary_symptoms.dyspnea: yes, progressive, initially with exertion then at rest

associated_symptoms.no_fever: yes, absence of fever is typical

exposures.occupational: asbestos, silica, coal dust, metal dust

physical_exam.general: thin, tachypneic, uses accessory muscles

respiratory.inspection: tachypneic, shallow breathing
respiratory.auscultation: bilateral fine inspiratory crackles (velcro crackles) at bases

cardiovascular.auscultation: may have loud P2 if pulmonary hypertension, RV heave

physical_exam.skin: may have findings of connective tissue disease

hrct_chest.result: usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern: subpleural, basal predominant reticular opacities, honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis
hrct_chest.interpretation: Characteristic findings allow diagnosis without biopsy

pulmonary_function_tests.result: restrictive pattern: reduced FVC and TLC, FEV1/FVC ratio normal or increased, reduced DLCO

chest_xray.result: bilateral reticular or reticulonodular opacities, reduced lung volumes, honeycombing if advanced

abg.result: hypoxemia, increased A-a gradient, normal or low CO2

autoimmune_panel.result: ANA, RF, anti-CCP if connective tissue disease

surgical_lung_biopsy.result: UIP pattern: patchy fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, honeycombing
surgical_lung_biopsy.interpretation: Gold standard but not always needed if classic HRCT

teaching_points: IPF is most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, median survival 3-5 years
UIP pattern on HRCT: subpleural, basilar reticular opacities with honeycombing
Treatment: antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib) slow progression but don't reverse fibrosis
Lung transplantation is only curative option
Velcro crackles (fine inspiratory crackles) are characteristic finding
key_features: Restrictive pattern on PFTs with reduced DLCO
UIP pattern on HRCT with honeycombing

name: Acute Bronchiolitis

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: wheezing and difficulty breathing in infant

patient_demographics.appearance: infant in respiratory distress, tachypneic, retractions

vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: 88-94% on room air if moderate to severe

physical_exam.general: alert but irritable, respiratory distress, nasal flaring

respiratory.inspection: subcostal and intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, head bobbing
respiratory.auscultation: diffuse expiratory wheezes, fine crackles, prolonged expiration, decreased air entry if severe

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, regular

physical_exam.hydration_status: assess mucous membranes, capillary refill, urine output

clinical_diagnosis.result: first episode of wheezing in infant <2 years with viral URI prodrome
clinical_diagnosis.interpretation: Clinical diagnosis, testing not routinely needed

rsv_rapid_antigen_or_pcr.interpretation: Confirms etiology but doesn't change management

chest_xray.result: hyperinflation, perihilar thickening, patchy atelectasis
chest_xray.interpretation: Only if suspect pneumonia or foreign body

viral_panel.result: RSV most common (50-80%), also rhinovirus, parainfluenza, influenza

teaching_points: RSV is most common cause (50-80% of cases), peak season November-March
Treatment is supportive: hydration, oxygen if needed, nasal suctioning
Bronchodilators and steroids NOT routinely effective
Hospitalization if: age <3 months, O2 sat <90%, poor feeding, apnea, or respiratory distress
Palivizumab (Synagis) prophylaxis for high-risk infants during RSV season
key_features: First wheezing episode in infant <2 years

name: Viral Pneumonia

patient_demographics.age_range: any age, more severe in young children and elderly

primary_symptoms.cough: yes, initially dry then may become productive

past_medical_history.immunosuppression: high risk for severe viral pneumonia

physical_exam.general: appears ill but not toxic, fatigued

respiratory.inspection: mildly increased work of breathing
respiratory.auscultation: scattered crackles or rhonchi, may have wheezes, bilateral and diffuse

cardiovascular.auscultation: tachycardic, regular

chest_xray.result: bilateral interstitial infiltrates, patchy opacities, peribronchial thickening, no lobar consolidation

viral_pcr_panel.result: positive for influenza, RSV, adenovirus, parainfluenza, rhinovirus, coronavirus

teaching_points: Most common viruses: influenza, RSV, adenovirus, parainfluenza
Interstitial (atypical) pattern on CXR vs lobar consolidation in bacterial
Treatment: supportive care, oseltamivir if influenza within 48 hours
Antibiotics NOT indicated unless bacterial superinfection suspected
Complications: bacterial superinfection (especially S. pneumoniae, S. aureus)
key_features: Fever with prominent myalgias and fatigue
Bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray
Low or normal WBC with lymphocytosis

name: Essential (Primary) Hypertension

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: routine check-up or elevated blood pressure reading

primary_symptoms.asymptomatic: yes, most patients have no symptoms

physical_exam.general: well-appearing, no acute distress

cardiovascular.palpation: PMI normal location unless LVH, no heaves
cardiovascular.auscultation: S4 sometimes if LVH, no murmurs unless complications

physical_exam.fundoscopic: AV nicking, arterial narrowing if chronic, papilledema if malignant HTN
physical_exam.abdominal: abdominal bruit if renal artery stenosis
physical_exam.extremities: pulses equal bilaterally, no edema unless heart failure

office_blood_pressure.interpretation: Diagnostic if elevated on multiple visits

ambulatory_blood_pressure_monitoring.interpretation: Gold standard, rules out white coat HTN

ecg.result: LVH (increased voltage, strain pattern) if chronic, or normal

echocardiogram.result: LV wall thickness >11mm, increased LV mass if chronic HTN

bmp.result: creatinine may be elevated, potassium normal or low

lipid_panel.result: variable, often elevated if metabolic syndrome

teaching_points: 90-95% of hypertension is essential (primary), no identifiable cause
JNC 8 guidelines: ≥130/80 is hypertension (2017 ACC/AHA)
First-line therapy: thiazide diuretic, ACE inhibitor, ARB, or CCB
Target BP <130/80 for most patients, individualize for elderly
10-year ASCVD risk calculator guides statin therapy

name: Acute Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)

patient_demographics.age_range: 50-70, can occur younger with risk factors
patient_demographics.appearance: appears severely distressed, diaphoretic, clutching chest

primary_symptoms.pain_radiation: left arm, jaw, neck, back, epigastrium

vital_signs.blood_pressure: variable: elevated 160/95 from pain, or low 90/60 if cardiogenic shock
vital_signs.heart_rate: variable: tachycardia 100-120, or bradycardia if inferior MI
vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: normal or decreased if pulmonary edema/shock

physical_exam.general: severe distress, diaphoretic, pale, anxious

cardiovascular.inspection: JVP elevated if RV infarct or failure
cardiovascular.palpation: PMI may be displaced if prior MI, no heaves

Emergency treatment: IV agents (nicardipine, labetalol, nitroprusside) to lower BP 10-20% in first hour, then 25% over 24 hours
Do NOT rapidly lower BP - can cause ischemic stroke, MI, or blindness
Target organs: hypertensive encephalopathy, stroke, acute MI, pulmonary edema, AKI, retinal hemorrhage, aortic dissection
key_features: Severe headache, confusion, or visual changes
Often precipitated by medication noncompliance or cocaine

name: Atrial Fibrillation

symptom_onset.timing: variable - may be sudden or gradual
symptom_onset.progression: episodes may increase in frequency over time

associated_symptoms.syncope: rare, concerning for rapid rate or pause
associated_symptoms.chest_pain: if concurrent CAD or demand ischemia
associated_symptoms.polyuria: sometimes due to atrial natriuretic peptide

medications: may already be on beta-blockers or other antihypertensives

social_history.exercise_habits: both extreme exercise and sedentary increase risk

vital_signs.respiratory_rate: 16-24, may be elevated if in distress
vital_signs.oxygen_saturation: usually normal unless heart failure present

physical_exam.general: alert, anxious, may appear uncomfortable

cardiovascular.inspection: may see JVP elevation if heart failure
cardiovascular.auscultation: irregularly irregular rhythm, variable S1 intensity, possible murmur if valvular disease

respiratory.inspection: assess for increased work of breathing
respiratory.auscultation: crackles if pulmonary edema, otherwise clear

ecg.result: irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves, fibrillatory waves, variable RR intervals

cbc.interpretation: Rule out anemia as contributing factor

troponin.result: usually normal, may be mildly elevated with demand

chest_xray.result: may show cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema if heart failure
chest_xray.interpretation: Assess heart size and pulmonary status

echocardiogram.result: may show left atrial enlargement, valvular disease, LV dysfunction, thrombus
echocardiogram.interpretation: Essential for structural assessment and pre-cardioversion

holter_monitor.result: documents paroxysmal episodes, burden of AFib
holter_monitor.interpretation: For suspected paroxysmal AFib not captured on ECG

Frequent_PACs: normal P waves intermixed with premature beats

essential_questions: stroke risk factors (HTN, DM, CHF, prior stroke, age)

teaching_points: Calculate CHA2DS2-VASc score for stroke risk: anticoagulate if ≥2 (men) or ≥3 (women)
Rate control (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers) vs rhythm control strategy
Anticoagulation decision separate from rate/rhythm control decision
TEE required before cardioversion if AFib >48 hours or unknown duration
NOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban) preferred over warfarin in most patients
Address reversible causes: alcohol, thyroid, electrolytes, sleep apnea
key_features: ECG showing no P waves and irregular RR intervals
Risk factors: age, hypertension, heart disease
Stroke risk assessment with CHA2DS2-VASc mandatory
Anticoagulation decision is critical management point

name: Cardiac Arrest

patient_demographics.appearance: unresponsive, pulseless, not breathing or agonal gasps

symptom_onset.progression: death within minutes if not resuscitated

initial_assessment.pulse_check: no carotid pulse - confirm within 10 seconds
initial_assessment.immediate_action: call code, start CPR, attach monitor/defibrillator

vital_signs.heart_rate: absent or see rhythm on monitor
vital_signs.temperature: check later for targeted temperature management

during_resuscitation.monitor_rhythm: VFib, pulseless VT, asystole, or PEA

post_rosc_if_achieved.targeted_exam: look for cause - trauma, drug use signs, surgical scars

cardiac_monitor.result: VFib (chaotic irregular waveform), pulseless VT (regular wide complex tachycardia), asystole (flatline), or PEA (organized rhythm without pulse)
cardiac_monitor.interpretation: Immediate - determines shockable vs non-shockable rhythm

ecg_post_rosc.result: may show STEMI, ischemic changes, old MI, Brugada pattern, long QT
ecg_post_rosc.interpretation: Identify reversible causes, guide post-arrest care

arterial_blood_gas.result: severe acidosis common (pH <7.0), hyperkalemia possible, hypoxemia

troponin.result: often elevated post-arrest, may indicate MI as cause

portable_chest_xray.result: check ETT placement, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly

bedside_ultrasound.result: cardiac activity (pseudo-PEA), pericardial effusion, RV strain (PE), pneumothorax
bedside_ultrasound.interpretation: Rapid assessment for reversible causes during CPR

ct_head.result: assess for hypoxic injury, hemorrhage if post-ROSC
ct_head.interpretation: Prognosis and cause determination after ROSC

coronary_angiography.result: may show acute occlusion if STEMI
coronary_angiography.interpretation: Post-ROSC if STEMI or high suspicion for ACS

PEA: organized electrical activity but no pulse

essential_actions: search for reversible causes (H's and T's)

teaching_points: High-quality CPR is most important intervention: rate 100-120/min, depth 2-2.4 inches, minimize interruptions
VFib/pulseless VT: immediate defibrillation, then CPR 2 min, then recheck
Asystole/PEA: CPR + epinephrine, search for reversible causes (H's and T's)
Epinephrine 1mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes during arrest
Amiodarone or lidocaine for refractory VFib/pulseless VT after 3rd shock
Post-ROSC: targeted temperature management, PCI if STEMI, ICU care, prognostication >72hr
Early bystander CPR and defibrillation dramatically improve survival
Avoid hyperventilation - worsens outcomes
key_features: Sudden collapse with loss of consciousness
Monitor shows VFib, pulseless VT, asystole, or PEA
Identify and treat reversible causes (H's and T's)

risk_stratification.afib: CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk, anticoagulation decision-making
risk_stratification.cardiac_arrest: downtime, witnessed status, initial rhythm prognosis

ecg_interpretation.afib: irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, fibrillatory waves
ecg_interpretation.svt: narrow complex regular tachycardia, P wave location
ecg_interpretation.vt: wide complex tachycardia, AV dissociation, Brugada criteria

emergency_management.afib: rate vs rhythm control, anticoagulation, cardioversion timing
emergency_management.vt: stable vs unstable, amiodarone vs cardioversion
emergency_management.cardiac_arrest: ACLS algorithms, high-quality CPR, H's and T's

long_term_management.afib: anticoagulation duration, rate control medications, ablation consideration
long_term_management.svt: lifestyle modification, prophylactic medications, catheter ablation
long_term_management.vt: ICD placement, antiarrhythmics, EP study, treat underlying disease
long_term_management.cardiac_arrest: post-ROSC care, targeted temperature management, prognostication

physical_examination: Rapid primary survey in cardiac arrest
therapeutic_decisions: Rate vs rhythm control in AFib

afib: Cardioverting without TEE or adequate anticoagulation
Treating rate and rhythm but forgetting anticoagulation
Not checking TSH for reversible cause
svt: Giving adenosine in WPW with AFib (can cause VFib)
Mistaking SVT with aberrancy for VT
Slow IV push of adenosine (must be rapid)
vt: Giving adenosine for wide complex tachycardia
Assuming SVT with aberrancy without considering VT
Not recognizing hemodynamic instability requiring immediate cardioversion
cardiac_arrest: Poor CPR quality (inadequate rate, depth, or recoil)
Not searching for reversible causes (H's and T's)

progressive_complexity.level_2_management: AFib - requires risk stratification and anticoagulation decisions
progressive_complexity.level_3_critical_care: VT - distinguish from SVT, assess stability, aggressive treatment
progressive_complexity.level_4_resuscitation: Cardiac arrest - ACLS protocols, team leadership, post-ROSC care
